summary: Describes a way to save bandwidth when exporting flow or packet records with IPFIX. Information shared by many records is sent once and kept separately from the details that differ. Because PSAMP packet reports are built on IPFIX, the same method applies to them.

eli5.summary: If every letter in a pile had the same long address, you could write the address once on a cover sheet. This note does that for network reports, so less data has to be sent.

questions: how to reduce ipfix export bandwidth
how does ipfix data reduction work
subtitle: Saving bandwidth when exporting network flow records by eliminating repeated data.

tldr.problem: When exporting flow records with IPFIX, many records contain the same values in certain fields (like source address), causing redundant data to be transmitted repeatedly across limited network bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The method separates fields that are common to multiple records (exported once with an identifier) from fields that are specific to each record (which reference the common data by ID), similar to using a footnote instead of repeating the same text on each page.
tldr.outcome: Bandwidth requirements can be reduced significantly, benefiting network monitoring systems constrained by export link capacity. The method works identically for both IPFIX flow records and PSAMP packet records.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: IPFIX flow records and PSAMP packet records

today: RFC 5473 is an Informational RFC providing guidance for reducing bandwidth in IPFIX and PSAMP deployments. It has not been obsoleted and remains useful for network operators deploying high-volume network monitoring.

sections.title: The Problem of Repeated Data
sections.content:
Network operators collect detailed information about IP traffic flows using IPFIX (IP Flow Information eXport), which allows devices like routers to report data about conversations on the network. A typical flow record might contain a source address, destination address, source port, destination port, byte count, packet count, and other details. When many flows share common attributes—for example, all flows from a particular server or through a particular interface—those common attributes get repeated in every single flow record exported.

This redundancy wastes bandwidth on the export path from the device generating the data to the collector that analyzes it. In high-traffic environments, the collector may receive millions of flow records per minute. If the same source address appears in ten thousand records, that address is encoded ten thousand times. The same problem occurs with PSAMP (Packet Sampling), which reports detailed information about sampled individual packets rather than aggregated flows.
sections.eli5: Imagine you have a pile of letters all going to the same address. You write the address on each letter. But you could write it once on a cover sheet and just number the letters. This RFC describes how to do that with network data.

sections.title: Separating Common From Specific Data
sections.content:
The method splits each flow record into two parts: Common Properties (attributes shared by multiple records) and Specific Properties (attributes unique to each record). Common Properties are exported once in a special data record with a unique identifier, called commonPropertiesID. Each Specific Properties record then contains only the fields that differ, plus a reference to the Common Properties ID. The receiver (collector) reassembles the complete record by combining the Specific Properties with the Common Properties from the matching ID.

For example, if 10,000 flow records all come from source address 192.0.2.1 and source port 443, the exporter creates one Common Properties record that includes the address and port, assigns it ID 27, and then each of the 10,000 specific records simply includes ID 27 plus the destination address, destination port, byte count, and other per-flow details. The data sent is roughly the size of one complete record plus 10,000 smaller records, instead of 10,000 complete records.
sections.eli5: Write the shared data (like source address) once in a template with an ID. Then each record just contains its unique data and says 'use template 27 for the rest'. The receiver glues them back together.

sections.title: Templates and Scope in IPFIX
sections.content:
IPFIX uses templates to describe the structure of exported data. The proposed method leverages a special type of template called an Options Template Record, which has a concept of scope. The scope defines the context in which the recorded data applies. For the data-reduction method, the commonPropertiesID is placed in the scope, meaning the Common Properties data record defines values for all data that shares that ID.

The exporter sends an Options Template Record describing the fields in the Common Properties (and that they are scoped by commonPropertiesID), then sends the actual Common Properties data records, then sends a regular Template Record describing the Specific Properties format. The Specific Properties records include the commonPropertiesID field so the collector knows which Common Properties row to retrieve. This structure is already defined in IPFIX and PSAMP protocols, so no changes to the base protocols are needed.
sections.eli5: IPFIX has a way to mark data as applying to a group via an ID (called scope). The method puts the common properties in such a group, gives the group an ID, and then each specific record says which group ID to use.

sections.title: Handling Different Transport Protocols
sections.content:
The method must account for whether the exporter uses SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol), TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), or UDP (User Datagram Protocol) to send data to the collector. With SCTP or TCP, which guarantee reliable in-order delivery, the exporter can send Common Properties records once and assumes they will always arrive. With UDP, which offers no guarantees, the exporter must resend Common Properties records periodically (the default is every 10 minutes) so that collectors that join the export stream partway through do not miss them.

The RFC also specifies that when an association is re-established (for TCP or SCTP), all active Common Properties must be resent. If a commonPropertiesID is no longer in use, the exporter can stop resending it. For UDP, the exporter must also avoid reusing an ID until sufficient time has passed to ensure the old ID is not mistakenly referenced by a delayed late-arriving record.
sections.eli5: With TCP and SCTP, you send the template once and you are done. With UDP, you send it again every 10 minutes because a late message might miss the first copy. When things reconnect, resend all the templates.

sections.title: Reassembly at the Collector
sections.content:
The collector (receiving device) stores the Common Properties records as it receives them and looks them up by ID when processing Specific Properties records. The RFC allows the collector to either store records separately and reconstruct them on demand, or reconstruct the full records in real time. Reconstruction is more complex because it requires maintaining an in-memory table of active Common Properties, but some collectors may prefer it to simplify downstream analytics.

The collector must handle several edge cases: if it receives a Specific Properties record before the corresponding Common Properties arrives, it should store the Specific record and await the Common Properties (which may arrive later or be retransmitted). If the collector receives a new Options Template Record with a commonPropertiesID it has already received without a withdrawal message, it must close the connection (this is a protocol error). When an SCTP association closes, all Common Properties from that association are discarded because the IDs are no longer valid.
sections.eli5: The collector remembers which data goes with each template ID. If a specific record arrives before its template, the collector waits for the template. If two templates claim the same ID without the first being withdrawn, something is wrong and the connection stops.
